text:
Anna Li: Quick q — where should I upload nsys / perfetto traces for the KV-cache perf regression? Also what metadata + redaction do we need? I captured a ~30s nsys that shows some kernel stalls and weird repeated KV loads.

Mike Chen: Upload to s3://redwood-internal-traces/eng-runtime/<team>/<YYYY-MM-DD>/ . Naming conv we use: <root_ts>-<owner>-<tool>-<model>-<short>.zip (eg `1732003456-anna-nsys-llama2-4k-kv.zip`). Try to keep each upload <500MB; if bigger, tar+split or upload the .nsys-rep and the smaller perfetto.pb separately. Include a meta.json next to the trace.

Raj Patel: Minimal meta fields: runtime_commit, model_name (canonical or obfuscated), deploy_config (batch_size, seq_len, quant), region, sample_trace_interval_ms, repro_cmd (if available). DO NOT include raw prompts or customer ids.

Anna Li: Got it. How do I redact? My nsys has S3 paths and full prompts in trace annotations.

Sara Gomez: We have a redaction helper under tools/redact_traces.py. It does 3 things: replaces S3 paths, scrubs UUIDs/customer-like ids, and truncates payload blobs longer than 200 chars. Example heuristics (run locally before upload):
```bash
# redact s3 paths and obvious customer IDs
python tools/redact_traces.py --in trace.nsys-rep --out trace.redacted.nsys-rep
# or a quick sed replacement for paths
sed -E 's#s3://[^[:space:]]+#<REDACTED_S3>#g' trace.nsys-rep > trace.redacted.nsys-rep
# replace long hex IDs
perl -pe 's/[A-Fa-f0-9]{12,}/<REDACTED_ID>/g' trace.redacted.nsys-rep > trace.final.nsys-rep
```
Patterns we target: `s3://[^ ]+ -> <REDACTED_S3>` and customer-id regexes like `[a-z0-9]{8}(-[a-z0-9]{4}){2,}` -> `<REDACTED_CUSTOMER_ID>`.

perf-bot: Reminder: you can also use the upload helper — `./bin/trace_upload --file=trace.zip --meta=meta.json --bucket=eng-runtime --prefix=priv/traces` — it will validate meta and return an internal link.

Mike Chen: When you upload, add an `annotations.txt` listing suspected hotspots and time ranges (ms relative to trace start). Example entry: `attention_fwd_kv_cache @ 1200-1450ms : repeated full KV loads, many host->device memcpy`. Also include the command used to collect the trace and the `git rev-parse HEAD` for the runtime.

Anna Li: What nsys flags are recommended? I used `nsys profile -o out --trace=cuda,osrt --sample=cpu` — is that enough?

Raj Patel: We generally prefer this pattern for full timeline + counters:
```bash
nsys profile \
  --output trace_1732003456 \
  --trace=cuda,osrt,cublas \
  --capture-range timeline \
  --capture-range-start=auto \
  --capture-range-end=stop \
  --force-overwrite \
  --stats=true
# For GPU metrics (via Nsight CLI), add gpu metrics collection if needed
nsys profile --capture-env --capture-range timeline --capture-range-end=stop --gpu-metrics sm_efficiency,achieved_occupancy
```
`nvprof` is legacy; prefer `nsys` + `perfetto` for cross-platform. For low-level counters we sometimes run `nvprof --metrics` on a repro.

Sara Gomez: Perfetto capture: `python -m perfetto trace --out=trace.pb --duration=30 --atrace --clear_cache` — or use the `perfetto` recorder on the host. Perfetto gives an easier kernel timeline and can be converted to Chrome trace for quick inspection.

Mike Chen: In analysis, watch for: long gaps between kernel launches (host-side stalls), high kernel launch overhead from many tiny kernels, excessive synchronous memcpy (`cudaMemcpySync`), and frequent kernel preemption. Use the nsys timeline and GPU Active/Idle metrics.

Anna Li: KV cache-specific: my trace shows repeated kv-cache loads for same key across requests when prefix cache should hit. I see repeated d2h/h2d copies.

Raj Patel: Likely causes: cache sharding mismatch (different worker IDs hashing same key incorrectly), eviction due to sequence-length miscalculation, or a cache-key construction bug. In the trace look for repeated identical device allocations or same-size memcopies from identical addresses. Grep the trace `.nsys-rep` for the key hash or for `cudaMemcpy` events.

Mike Chen: Batching heuristics: compute inter-arrival histogram from the trace (timestamps of request enqueue). If arrival spacing > batching window you'll get a lot of single-request launches. If arrival spacing << window but you still see single-run kernels, check the batching worker's readiness checks and preemption. Consider enabling continuous batching or increasing batching window in config.

Sara Gomez: Upload naming examples we use internally: `1732003456-anna-nsys-opt-kvcache.zip` and inside: `trace.nsys-rep`, `trace.perfetto.pb`, `meta.json`, `annotations.txt`, `repro.sh`. Example meta.json keys: `runtime_commit`, `deploy_config`, `trace_tool`, `trace_duration_ms`, `uploader`, `notes`.

Anna Li: Uploaded `1732003456-anna-nsys-opt-kvcache.zip` to `s3://redwood-internal-traces/eng-runtime/2024-11-09/` (perf-bot reports upload id 99823). Link: <internal link>. @Mike @Raj please take a look.

Mike Chen: Looking now. Quick scan: I see `softmax_fwd` which is 12ms and ~6 matmul kernels around it, and a top kernel `attention_fwd_nv_k` at ~42% GPU time. There are also a bunch of 100-300us kernels which add up to launch overhead. Could be missing fusion or wrong kernel selector picked a generic kernel.

Anna Li: Attached `.nsys-rep` and reduced `perfetto.pb`. I put `annotations.txt` with suspected ranges.

Raj Patel: I ran a quick summary: attention_fwd_nv_k ~42% GPU time, softmax_fwd ~18%, kernel launch overhead ~8%. Memcpy churn between attention and softmax suggests repeated KV flush. Try these experiments: 1) enable persistent kernel for attention, 2) increase micro-batch window, 3) force alternative kernel selection (debug flag) to the fused attention path and re-run small trace.

Mike Chen: If you want us to reproduce, include a minimal repro harness (run_repro.sh) and a small tokenized sample. Put it in the same folder and mark it `internal-only`. We'll run it on a consistent node and attach our traces.

Anna Li: Thanks — I'll run a repro with `PERSISTENT_KERNEL=1` and post the new traces as `1732005678-anna-repro-persistent-kernel.zip`. Will redact and update meta. :eyes:
